title: Sharding / Partitioning
subtitle: Partition data and traffic across machines while managing skew and cross-shard work
objectives: Explain when replication stops being enough and splitting is the only option left
Choose a shard key, and predict the hot shard it will create
Compare range and hash partitioning, and explain what consistent hashing solves
Account for what sharding costs: cross-shard queries, transactions, and resharding

exercises.title: Sharding routes each record to one partition using a shard key
exercises.body: A sharding rule reads a shard key, such as `user_id`, and maps each record to one database partition. Reads and writes that include the key route to that partition. Because partitions hold disjoint subsets, write load and storage can be distributed across machines.
exercises.note: Replication must still be configured within each shard for redundancy. Without replicas, losing one shard makes its entire subset unavailable.

exercises.prompt: One database receives 12,000 independent user writes per second but handles 5,000. Hash users across three shards.
exercises.afterStatus: WRITE LOAD · approximately 4,000 / 5,000 writes/s per shard
exercises.result: The write load spread across three owners
exercises.why: Hashing a well-distributed user ID can spread independent user writes across shards. The result is approximate: celebrity traffic or a poor key can still create a hot shard, and cross-shard queries become more expensive.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: One database receives 12,000 independent user writes per second but handles 5,000. Hash users across three shards. Place Shard router, Shard 1, Shard 2. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Application → Shard router; Shard router → Shard 1; Shard router → Shard 2; Shard router → Shard 3. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Hashing a well-distributed user ID can spread independent user writes across shards. The result is approximate: celebrity traffic or a poor key can still create a hot shard, and cross-shard queries become more expensive.

exercises.prompt: Your database is drowning in WRITES. You add five read replicas. Does it help?
choices: Yes — five more machines share the work
No — every replica must apply every write, so you've added five machines that each do all the writing and none that do less
Yes, if you route writes to the replicas
exercises.why: Each replica must apply the complete write stream to remain a copy of the dataset. Adding five read replicas creates more read-serving capacity but does not divide database writes, and replication transport can add work to the leader.

exercises.prompt: ______ splits your data across machines so each one holds only a subset of it.
exercises.why: Sharding partitions rows by a deterministic rule so each shard stores only its assigned subset. This division lets storage and request work be distributed across machines.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to what it does.

pairs.right: Every machine holds all the data
Each machine holds a slice of the data
Writes, reads, and total data size

exercises.why: Replication places the full dataset on each copy and provides additional read paths and redundancy. Sharding places different subsets on different machines and divides reads, writes, and storage; each shard still needs replication if it must survive a machine failure.

exercises.prompt: Which problems does sharding actually solve? Select all.
choices: A dataset too large to fit on one machine
exercises.why: Sharding assigns each machine a subset of rows, so writes and reads for different subsets can run in parallel and total stored data can exceed one machine's capacity. A single copy of each shard remains a failure risk; replication is required to preserve that shard's data and availability.

exercises.prompt: You shard users across 4 machines. Where does user 12345 live?
choices: On whichever machine is least busy
Wherever the shard key says — a rule maps that user's id to exactly one shard, and everyone applies the same rule
exercises.why: The shard key is the input to a deterministic placement rule. Readers and writers use that rule, directly or through a router, to locate user 12345 without probing every shard; changing the key later requires relocating data to match the new mapping.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'don't shard until you have to' such common advice?
choices: Because it permanently costs you cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions, and painful resharding — costs you pay daily, for a scale you may not have
Because databases can't be sharded safely
exercises.why: Sharding makes the placement key part of the data layout and turns multi-shard queries and transactions into distributed operations. Those costs apply to development and operation immediately, so sharding is justified when measured write throughput or storage size is approaching one machine's limit.

exercises.title: Range partitioning assigns contiguous shard-key intervals to machines
exercises.body: In range partitioning, the router compares a shard key with ordered boundaries: keys in one interval go to shard A, the next interval to shard B, and so on. Range queries on the shard key can target only shards whose intervals overlap the requested range.
exercises.note: Range boundaries can produce uneven load when inserted keys cluster in one part of the key space, even if stored records are balanced overall.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Range partitioning assigns contiguous shard-key intervals to machines
exercises.why: In range partitioning, the router compares a shard key with ordered boundaries: keys in one interval go to shard A, the next interval to shard B, and so on. Range queries on the shard key can target only shards whose intervals overlap the requested range. Range boundaries can produce uneven load when inserted keys cluster in one part of the key space, even if stored records are balanced overall.

exercises.prompt: You shard by user_id using ranges: users 1–1M on shard A, 1M–2M on B, and so on. Your ids auto-increment. What happens?
choices: Every new signup lands on the newest shard, so all your write traffic hammers one machine while the others idle
Old shards get all the writes
exercises.why: Auto-incrementing identifiers increase into the highest active range, so all new user rows map to the shard owning that range. The other shards may serve older data, while the newest shard receives the entire signup write stream and becomes a hot shard.

exercises.prompt: Match each partitioning strategy to its behaviour.

pairs.right: Ordered slices — keeps range queries fast
Sequential keys create a hot shard
'All rows between X and Y' now hits every shard

exercises.why: Range partitioning preserves key order, so a range query can target adjacent shards, while monotonic writes can concentrate on one range. Hash partitioning spreads keys by hash value, improving distribution while removing the ordering needed to localize range queries.

exercises.prompt: You hash `user_id` to pick a shard. What did that fix, and what did it break?
choices: Sequential user writes now spread across shards, but a query for user IDs 1M–2M must scatter because hashing no longer preserves adjacent ID ranges
It fixed everything with no cost
It broke writes but fixed reads
exercises.why: A suitable hash distributes sequential user IDs across hash ranges, preventing the newest IDs from concentrating writes on one range shard. The cost is that adjacent `user_id` values no longer share a shard, so a range query on that actual shard key must contact every shard and merge results.

exercises.prompt: A chat app shards messages by hash(message_id). Loading one conversation is now slow. Why?
choices: The hash is slow to compute
A conversation's messages are scattered across every shard, so reading one chat means querying all of them
The shard key is too long
exercises.why: Hashing each message identifier independently scatters one conversation's messages across shards. Loading the conversation therefore requires scatter-gather, meaning parallel queries to all shards followed by a merge; using `conversation_id` could keep that access pattern local to one shard.

exercises.prompt: So what's the rule for choosing a shard key?
choices: Pick something with many distinct values that spreads load evenly AND matches how you query, so your common reads stay on one shard
exercises.why: A useful shard key has enough distinct values and an appropriate distribution to avoid concentrating load, while aligning with common query predicates so those queries target one shard. A key that satisfies only distribution can force frequent fan-out, and a localizing key with skew can create hotspots.

exercises.prompt: You shard a multi-tenant SaaS app by tenant_id. What should worry you?
choices: Tenants aren't the same size: one enormous customer can outgrow a single shard, and no amount of rebalancing splits one tenant
exercises.why: Using `tenant_id` keeps tenant-scoped queries on one shard, but the placement rule treats each tenant as an indivisible unit. A very large or busy tenant can exceed one shard's storage or throughput; a composite key can add subdivisions when that risk must be supported.

exercises.title: Request skew can overload a shard whose key count is evenly distributed
exercises.body: Hash partitioning can assign similar numbers of keys to each shard. Runtime load equals the sum of request rates for those keys, so one frequently accessed key can saturate its shard while every shard stores the same number of records.
exercises.note: Moving unrelated keys cannot divide traffic for one hot key. Common mitigations cache its reads or split its workload with a finer composite key.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Request skew can overload a shard whose key count is evenly distributed
exercises.why: Hash partitioning can assign similar numbers of keys to each shard. Runtime load equals the sum of request rates for those keys, so one frequently accessed key can saturate its shard while every shard stores the same number of records. Moving unrelated keys cannot divide traffic for one hot key. Common mitigations cache its reads or split its workload with a finer composite key.

exercises.prompt: You shard a social app by user_id. One user has 200 million followers. What breaks?
choices: Everything about that user lives on one shard, so that machine takes a wildly disproportionate share of traffic — a hot shard
exercises.why: Hashing can distribute key counts evenly while one key receives far more requests than the others. Because all activity for the celebrity key maps to one shard, that shard becomes the throughput bottleneck; mitigation may cache those reads or subdivide that key's workload.

exercises.prompt: You have 4 shards, assigned by hash(key) % 4. You add a fifth machine, making it % 5. What happens?
choices: Only the new shard's data moves
Almost every key now maps somewhere new, so the vast majority of your data has to move at once
exercises.why: The remainder of `hash(key) % 5` differs from `hash(key) % 4` for most hash values. Most keys therefore receive a new shard assignment, forcing a large online data migration and routing transition when the fifth shard is added.

exercises.prompt: What does consistent hashing fix about that?
choices: Adding one node to a balanced ring of n old nodes remaps roughly 1/(n+1) of the keys instead of nearly all of them
It removes the need for a shard key
exercises.why: Consistent hashing places keys and node positions on a ring and assigns each key to the next node position. Adding one node to `n` old balanced nodes creates `n+1` shares and captures about `1/(n+1)` of the keys; removing one of `n` nodes moves about `1/n`. It does not divide one exceptionally hot key.

exercises.prompt: Consistent hashing with few nodes distributes data unevenly. What's the standard fix?
choices: Virtual nodes — place each machine at many points on the ring, so the averaging smooths out the arcs
exercises.why: With one ring position per machine, random gaps between positions can give machines unequal key ranges. Virtual nodes assign each physical machine many positions, averaging those small ranges into a more even share and spreading a departing machine's ranges across multiple peers.

exercises.prompt: How does an application know which shard to talk to?
choices: It computes the rule itself, or asks a routing layer or directory that knows the current mapping
exercises.why: A client can compute a stable placement rule locally, or it can query a routing layer or directory that stores the current mapping. Local computation avoids a routing hop but couples deployments to mapping changes; a directory supports movable shards but must be consistent, available, and itself redundant.

exercises.prompt: Order a shard migration that stays online without relying on non-atomic dual writes.
steps: Start durable change data capture on the old shard and record its log position
Backfill a consistent snapshot tied to that log position while writes continue on the old shard
Replay captured changes with idempotent upserts until the new shard catches up
Briefly quiesce writes, apply the final log tail, and verify counts and checksums
Switch reads and writes to the new shard, then resume traffic
Keep the old shard read-only as a rollback copy until the new placement is proven
exercises.why: Change data capture records every committed old-shard mutation in a durable ordered log, closing the gap created while the snapshot is copied. Catch-up plus a brief write pause establishes a verified cutover point; retaining the old shard read-only preserves rollback without allowing two independent writable copies to diverge.

lessons.title: A balanced dataset can still have a hot shard

exercises.title: Traffic—not row count—determines whether a shard is hot
exercises.body: A shard holding one celebrity can receive most profile reads even when every shard stores the same number of rows. Splitting or replicating that hot key moves part of its read traffic away from one primary bottleneck; ordinary keys can keep their existing placement.
exercises.note: Write authority still needs one defined path. This simulation moves read traffic, not concurrent writes.

exercises.prompt: One celebrity generates 24,000 reads/s on a shard that handles 6,000. Drag the *smallest* share of that key's reads to replicated read buckets that keeps the hot shard alive.

absorb.label: Reads shifted from the hot shard

exercises.why: Shifting 75% sends 18,000 reads/s elsewhere and leaves exactly 6,000 on the original shard. This relieves a read hotspot; it does not remove the need to route writes and invalidations correctly.

exercises.title: Queries without a routable shard key use scatter-gather
exercises.body: When a query does not constrain the shard key, the router cannot select one partition. It sends the query to every relevant shard, waits for their partial results, and merges them. This fan-out and merge operation is called scatter-gather.
exercises.note: When the result requires every shard response, scatter-gather waits for its slowest shard and also pays routing and merge overhead. More fan-out raises the chance that one shard contributes a tail-latency response.

exercises.prompt: Build the scatter-gather path for `count all users who signed up today`. The query lacks the shard key, so the routing layer must fan out to every partition shown.
exercises.why: Because the predicate does not include the shard key, the router lacks enough information to choose one partition; it sends the query to every shard and merges their partial counts. Completion waits for the slowest required shard, and one unavailable shard can make the global count unavailable or incomplete unless the product explicitly accepts a partial result.

exercises.prompt: You need to transfer money between two users who live on different shards, atomically. How hard is that?
choices: Easy — wrap it in a transaction
Hard: strict atomicity needs distributed commit such as two-phase commit, or a redesign that colocates the ledger entries on one transactional shard
exercises.why: A local database transaction cannot atomically commit changes owned by two independent shards. Two-phase commit can coordinate one all-or-nothing outcome, with blocking and coordinator failure modes. Colocating both ledger entries avoids cross-shard commit. A saga exposes intermediate committed states and compensation, so it cannot provide the strict atomicity required here.

exercises.prompt: Which get harder once you shard? Select all.
choices: Joins between tables on different shards
Looking up a single row by shard key
exercises.why: Cross-shard queries and joins must contact and combine data from multiple machines, while cross-shard transactions require a distributed commit or compensation protocol. A lookup by shard key remains local because the router can select exactly one shard.

exercises.prompt: A year in, you realize you sharded by the wrong key. How bad is that?
choices: Severe: the key determined where every row physically lives, so changing it means relocating the entire dataset while serving traffic
exercises.why: The shard key determines the machine responsible for every row. Changing it assigns many existing rows to different machines, so the system must copy and verify data, handle concurrent writes, update routing, and cut traffic over while remaining online.

exercises.prompt: Your app is read-heavy, fits comfortably on one machine, but reads are overwhelming it. Should you shard?
choices: Yes — sharding is how you scale
No — the data fits and writes are fine, so caching and read replicas solve this without any of sharding's costs
Only if you have more than a million users
exercises.why: The dataset fits and write capacity is sufficient, so partitioning does not address the stated constraints. Caching can absorb repeated reads and read replicas can add read-serving capacity without introducing shard routing, cross-shard queries, or cross-shard transactions.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of sharding?
choices: It's how real systems scale, so do it early
It's the only way past one machine's write and storage limits — and it costs you cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions, and a key you can't easily change
It's obsolete now that machines are large
exercises.why: Sharding partitions writes and stored bytes across machines, allowing the system to exceed one database's write and storage limits. The placement key becomes structural, and operations spanning placements require scatter-gather or distributed transaction coordination, so the benefit must justify those continuing costs.

exercises.prompt: A game shards inventory by `player_id`, but a global query asks for every copy of one rare item. What cost appears?
exercises.why: The query lacks the shard key and the target rows are distributed by player, so the router must ask many shards and merge their responses.
